findings.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/createOAuthAppCredential.ts:30 — The team branch allows any accepted member to create team-owned OAuth credentials and bypasses the admin-access guard, enabling unauthorized shared integrations.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — The sync path returns a Fetch `Response`, while Google and HubSpot expect parsed provider-specific objects; credential-sync refreshes therefore fail.
packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97 — The entire `{success, data}` parse envelope is persisted instead of its data, corrupting the stored Google credential after one refresh.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:5 — Computed Zod properties become literal keys rather than wildcard validation, stripping expiry and provider fields from synchronized tokens.
packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:75 — Salesforce refresh bypasses `refreshOAuthTokens`, so it does not participate in the advertised centralized credential-sync flow.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/decodeOAuthState.ts:9 — OAuth state is trusted as unsigned caller-controlled JSON without a session-bound nonce, permitting account-linking CSRF and `teamId` tampering.
packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/createOAuthAppCredential.ts:38 — Any accepted team member can attach team-owned credentials because the admin check is bypassed whenever `teamId` is present.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — Token-returning sync requests contain only predictable user/app identifiers and no shared-secret header or signature, allowing forged refresh requests if the endpoint is reachable.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:15 — The two branches expose incompatible contracts—raw Fetch response versus provider-specific values—so the documented minimal sync response cannot satisfy existing callers.
packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97 — Google persists the safe-parse wrapper rather than `.data`, drifting the credential shape and breaking subsequent authentication.
packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:8 — The minimum response schema strips normal expiry fields instead of preserving them, violating the advertised sync response contract.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:15 — Validation is selected from global configuration rather than the response source, so direct Salesforce responses are parsed as minimal sync responses and lose required fields.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:25 — Missing refresh tokens are replaced with literal `"refresh_token"`, overwriting real credentials and breaking fallback to provider refresh.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:15 — Sync mode returns a raw response to incompatible callers; Google masks the exception and HubSpot swallows failure before continuing with stale or unset authentication.
packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97 — Persisting the parser envelope durably breaks Google credentials after their first ordinary refresh.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:5 — Invalid wildcard schema construction strips metadata and injects a dummy refresh token, making Office 365 and Salesforce credentials unusable.
packages/app-store/office365video/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:87 — A successful minimal sync response replaces the entire credential key, discarding refresh token, email, scope, and provider metadata.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — The shared external refresh request has no abort deadline or bounded transient-failure handling, allowing one stalled service to block all dependent integrations.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — No contract test covers provider-specific return shapes; synchronized Google and HubSpot refreshes are already incompatible with the helper’s raw response.
packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97 — No persistence test asserts the stored Google credential shape, allowing the `{success, data}` wrapper corruption to ship.
packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:5 — No unit test verifies preservation of expiry and provider fields in a representative sync response.

apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:24 — No negative test covers both webhook secret and request header being absent; `undefined === undefined` authenticates the request when sharing is enabled.

packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:96 — No service test verifies that the newly refreshed Salesforce access token is used by the constructed client; the implementation uses the old token.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:3 — The shared refresher erases its return type with `any`, preventing the compiler from detecting its incompatible provider and Fetch response contracts.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:13 — The type-erased parser throws on failure but returns a safe-parse envelope, producing inconsistent consumer behavior, credential corruption, and dead branches.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:8 — The attempted generic schema uses unsupported computed keys and cannot preserve the fields required by the integrations it centralizes.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:15 — Ambient global configuration selects validation independently of acquisition, silently coupling provider responses to the wrong schema.

packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:75 — Salesforce duplicates a direct provider refresh while consuming the configuration-sensitive shared parser, causing policy drift and excluding it from sync.

packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:96 — The new Salesforce path calls `prisma.credential.update` without importing or defining `prisma`, causing a build-blocking unresolved identifier.
packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:13 — Raw sync responses are consumed as provider objects; Google stays expired and HubSpot may continue using stale module-global client state.
packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97 — Persisting the safe-parse wrapper removes top-level OAuth fields and breaks Google authentication after the first refresh.
packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:8 — The minimum schema silently discards expiration and provider metadata, causing refresh loops and incomplete persisted credentials.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:9 — The sync request identifies credentials only by user and app despite multiple credentials being allowed, so it can refresh the wrong external account.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — The token-returning sync endpoint is called without caller authentication, exposing fresh OAuth tokens to forged predictable-ID requests if reachable.
apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:73 — Credential updates have no event ID, version, timestamp, or compare-and-swap guard, allowing replayed or delayed webhooks to overwrite newer keys.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:25 — The fabricated refresh-token sentinel overwrites Office 365’s valid token, preventing direct refresh if synchronization is disabled or unavailable.

packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:101 — The Salesforce connection is constructed with the stale pre-refresh access token, so the current operation can still fail after successful refresh.
apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62 — Non-atomic `findFirst` followed by `create` permits concurrent first deliveries to create duplicate credentials.

packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:75 — Every Salesforce service construction performs an unconditional remote refresh and database write, adding latency, write amplification, and throttling risk.
apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:31 — Throwing schema parsing is not translated into a defined 4xx response, so malformed client payloads receive internal-server errors.
apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:17 — The mutating webhook does not constrain its HTTP method or return `405`/`Allow`, leaving callers without a stable method contract.
apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62 — The non-atomic lookup/create flow and lack of uniqueness serialization allow duplicate credentials and arbitrary stale-row updates.
apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:73 — Blind arrival-order updates allow delayed retries to overwrite newer credentials with older or revoked tokens.
apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:31 — Validation, decryption, and JSON parsing failures are not mapped to 4xx responses, encouraging retries of poison requests and obscuring diagnosis.

packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:75 — Salesforce refreshes unconditionally without a timeout and uses exact `statusText === "OK"` rather than `response.ok`, rejecting otherwise valid responses.

apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:31 — No request tests cover malformed bodies, invalid ciphertext, unsupported methods, or invalid decrypted JSON, leaving the endpoint’s error contract unprotected.
apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62 — No idempotency or concurrency test covers the separate lookup/create flow and resulting duplicate-credential risk.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/createOAuthAppCredential.ts:30 — Team authorization is duplicated inline while the shared admin guard is effectively dead for team credentials, creating divergent policy and unnecessary member materialization.
apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62 — Concurrent first-time deliveries can create duplicates, after which later updates affect only an arbitrary credential row.
packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:25 — Mutating an omitted refresh token into the literal sentinel permanently breaks later provider fallback.

packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:101 — Salesforce persists refreshed tokens but initializes the current connection from the stale credential snapshot, yielding misleading persisted health and active-client failure.
packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — The external refresh dependency has no timeout, retry policy, status gate, or provider fallback, creating a broad cascade-failure point.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/createOAuthAppCredential.ts:42 — The membership-existence query selects every team member although only `team.id` is used, causing unbounded relation materialization for large teams.

goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — Token-returning sync requests contain only predictable user/app identifiers and no shared-secret header or signature, allowing forged refresh requests if the endpoint is reachable.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the refreshOAuthTokens function in packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts, when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is set, it makes a POST request to the sync endpoint with only calcomUserId and appSlug in the body. There is no authentication header, signature, or shared secret being sent with this outgoing request. This is different from the incoming webhook (app-credential.ts) which does verify CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET. The finding correctly identifies that the outgoing sync request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT lacks authentication, meaning if an attacker knows the endpoint URL, they could potentially forge requests. However, this is an outgoing request to a self-hosted endpoint that the user controls, and the security model appears to rely on the endpoint being private/internal. The finding has merit but the severity depends on deployment context.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:15 — The two branches expose incompatible contracts—raw Fetch response versus provider-specific values—so the documented minimal sync response cannot satisfy existing callers.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at refreshOAuthTokens.ts, when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true, it returns the raw fetch Response object directly (line 14: `return response`). When false, it returns `await refreshFunction()` which could be anything the caller's function returns. The callers in the diff (e.g., GoogleCalendarService, Office365CalendarService) expect to work with the response data. In GoogleCalendarService line 91-92, it does `const token = res?.data` expecting the response to have a `.data` property. A raw fetch Response doesn't have `.data` - it has `.json()` method. However, looking more carefully at the sync branch, it fetches from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT and returns the Response object. The caller then tries to access `.data` on it which would be undefined. This is a real incompatibility - the sync path returns a Fetch Response while callers expect the original provider's response format with `.data` property.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97 — Google persists the safe-parse wrapper rather than `.data`, drifting the credential shape and breaking subsequent authentication.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for GoogleCalendarService.ts, line 97 shows `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);`. The parseRefreshTokenResponse function (defined in parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts) returns the result of `schema.safeParse(response)` which is a SafeParseReturnType object containing `{success: boolean, data?: T, error?: ZodError}`. This wrapper object is then stored directly as the credential key via `data: { key }` on line 99. Previously, the code used `const key = googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` which returns the actual parsed data, not a wrapper. This is indeed a bug - the credential shape will be wrong (containing success/data/error properties instead of the actual credential fields), which will break subsequent authentication attempts.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:8 — The minimum response schema strips normal expiry fields instead of preserving them, violating the advertised sync response contract.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts file, the minimumTokenResponseSchema on lines 5-11 is incorrectly defined. The syntax `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` is not valid Zod schema syntax for defining dynamic keys. This would result in literal string keys like '[object Object]' rather than allowing arbitrary string keys. However, the finding claims the schema 'strips normal expiry fields' - this is not accurate. The schema only requires access_token and attempts (incorrectly) to allow other properties. The real issue is the invalid Zod syntax, not that it strips fields. The schema is used with safeParse which would still parse the response, and the code later checks for refresh_token and adds a placeholder if missing. The finding's specific claim about 'stripping normal expiry fields' and 'violating the advertised sync response contract' is not precisely what's happening - the schema syntax is wrong but the actual behavior would be different than described.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:15 — Validation is selected from global configuration rather than the response source, so direct Salesforce responses are parsed as minimal sync responses and lose required fields.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts, the function checks APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT to decide whether to use minimumTokenResponseSchema or the passed schema. The issue is that when credential sharing is enabled globally, ALL refresh token responses (including direct Salesforce responses) would be parsed with the minimal schema instead of the app-specific schema. However, examining the actual usage in the diff - GoogleCalendarService passes googleCredentials (not the response) to parseRefreshTokenResponse, and Office365CalendarService uses it correctly. The Salesforce CalendarService diff is truncated but shows salesforceTokenSchema being defined. The finding has merit - the global config determines validation rather than the response source, which could cause issues. But looking more carefully, the logic seems intentional: when credential sync is enabled, the external endpoint handles token refresh and returns minimal tokens, so minimal validation is appropriate. When disabled, the app's own refresh logic runs and needs full validation. This appears to be by design, not a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:25 — Missing refresh tokens are replaced with literal `"refresh_token"`, overwriting real credentials and breaking fallback to provider refresh.
matched_golden_ids: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: the parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the literal string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the response. Both comments point to the same file, same line (25), and describe the same consequence - breaking token refresh functionality by overwriting/invalidating credentials.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:15 — Sync mode returns a raw response to incompatible callers; Google masks the exception and HubSpot swallows failure before continuing with stale or unset authentication.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at refreshOAuthTokens.ts, when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true, it returns the raw fetch Response object. When false, it returns the result of refreshFunction(). The callers expect different return types: GoogleCalendarService expects res.data with token properties, Office365CalendarService calls handleErrorsJson(response), etc. However, examining the actual usage in GoogleCalendarService (line 83-95), when credential sync is enabled, the response from the external endpoint should contain the token data directly. The function returns either the fetch Response or the refreshFunction result - both are Response-like objects that callers handle. The finding claims 'Google masks the exception' but the code shows proper error handling with try/catch. The finding about 'incompatible callers' has some merit - the return type inconsistency could cause issues, but the callers appear to handle Response objects appropriately. The claim about HubSpot 'swallowing failure' isn't clearly demonstrated in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97 — Persisting the parser envelope durably breaks Google credentials after their first ordinary refresh.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for GoogleCalendarService.ts, line 97 shows `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);`. The parseRefreshTokenResponse function returns a SafeParseReturnType object (the result of calling `.safeParse()`), not the actual parsed data. This object has structure like `{success: true, data: {...}}` or `{success: false, error: ...}`. The code then passes this envelope object directly to `prisma.credential.update()` as the `key` field, instead of extracting `.data` from it. This would indeed corrupt the stored credentials by saving the wrong structure. The original code was `const key = googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials);` which returns the actual parsed data directly. This is a real bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:5 — Invalid wildcard schema construction strips metadata and injects a dummy refresh token, making Office 365 and Salesforce credentials unusable.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts lines 5-10, the schema construction `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` is indeed problematic. `z.string().toString()` returns a string representation of the Zod schema object (like '[object Object]'), not a dynamic key pattern. This creates a schema with literal keys like '[object Object]' rather than allowing arbitrary string keys. Additionally, line 24-26 unconditionally sets `refresh_token = 'refresh_token'` if it's missing, which would inject a dummy value. However, looking at the actual usage in Office365CalendarService.ts line 256, the function returns the result of `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)`, and the code then uses `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data`. The schema issue is real - the minimumTokenResponseSchema won't work as intended for validating arbitrary OAuth responses because the wildcard key syntax is incorrect in Zod.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/office365video/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:87 — A successful minimal sync response replaces the entire credential key, discarding refresh token, email, scope, and provider metadata.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for packages/app-store/office365video/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts, I can see that refreshOAuthTokens is now being used to wrap the fetch call (lines 61-76), but the code after this (handling responseBody and updating credentials) is not shown in the diff - it's truncated. The diff only shows the refreshOAuthTokens wrapper being added, not how the response is processed afterward. Without seeing the credential update logic, I cannot confirm this is a real issue. Additionally, looking at parseRefreshTokenResponse in the new file, it does add a placeholder refresh_token if missing (line 26-28), which suggests some awareness of this issue. The finding is speculative about behavior not clearly shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — The shared external refresh request has no abort deadline or bounded transient-failure handling, allowing one stalled service to block all dependent integrations.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the refreshOAuthTokens function in packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts, the fetch call to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT has no timeout, abort signal, or retry logic. However, this is a new feature for credential syncing with external services. The finding claims this could 'block all dependent integrations' but this is speculative - the function is called per-credential refresh, not in a way that would block other integrations. Additionally, the lack of timeout on fetch calls is a common pattern in this codebase (looking at other fetch calls in the diff). While adding a timeout would be a good practice, the finding overstates the impact. The code works correctly for its intended purpose; the lack of timeout is a potential improvement rather than a clear defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — No contract test covers provider-specific return shapes; synchronized Google and HubSpot refreshes are already incompatible with the helper’s raw response.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a real architectural issue. Looking at the diff, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw response from either the custom endpoint or the refreshFunction. For Google Calendar (line 86-98), the response is `res?.data` from myGoogleAuth.refreshToken(). For HubSpot (line 176-191), it returns a HubspotToken object directly from hubspotClient.oauth.tokensApi.createToken(). For Office365 (line 246-262), it returns a fetch Response object. These are fundamentally different return types - Google returns the inner data, HubSpot returns a token object, Office365 returns a Response that needs .json() called. The helper function at line 8-21 doesn't normalize these different shapes, and there are no tests ensuring the provider-specific returns are compatible. This is a real correctness issue where the abstraction doesn't properly handle the different return types from different OAuth providers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97 — No persistence test asserts the stored Google credential shape, allowing the `{success, data}` wrapper corruption to ship.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for GoogleCalendarService.ts, line 97 shows `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);`. The parseRefreshTokenResponse function (defined in parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts) returns the result of `schema.safeParse(response)`, which is a Zod SafeParseReturnType object with `{success, data}` structure. This object is then directly stored as the credential key via `data: { key }`. This is indeed a bug - the code should be storing `key.data` (the actual parsed data) rather than `key` (the wrapper object). However, the finding is about 'no persistence test' which is about missing tests, not about the actual bug in the code. The real issue is the code bug, not the lack of tests. The finding is somewhat misdirected - it identifies a symptom (lack of tests) rather than the actual defect (storing wrong object shape).

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:5 — No unit test verifies preservation of expiry and provider fields in a representative sync response.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is about missing unit tests for the parseRefreshTokenResponse function. While the function does have potential issues (the schema definition with dynamic keys is incorrect and won't work as intended), the specific finding about 'no unit test verifies preservation of expiry and provider fields' is a test coverage concern, not a bug in the code itself. Missing tests are not a 'real problem' in the sense of a bug, security issue, or correctness problem in the actual code - they're a quality/coverage concern. The diff shows new code being added, and while tests would be valuable, their absence doesn't constitute a defect in the code that was written.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:24 — No negative test covers both webhook secret and request header being absent; `undefined === undefined` authenticates the request when sharing is enabled.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code at line 24: `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || 'calcom-webhook-secret'] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. If CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is not set (undefined) and the header is also not present in the request (undefined), then `undefined !== undefined` evaluates to `false`, meaning the check passes and the request is authenticated. This is a real security vulnerability - when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true but CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is not configured, any request without the header would be authenticated.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:96 — No service test verifies that the newly refreshed Salesforce access token is used by the constructed client; the implementation uses the old token.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:3 — The shared refresher erases its return type with `any`, preventing the compiler from detecting its incompatible provider and Fetch response contracts.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for refreshOAuthTokens.ts, the function signature is `async (refreshFunction: () => any, appSlug: string, userId: number | null)` and returns `Promise<any>`. The finding claims this 'erases return type with any, preventing compiler from detecting incompatible provider and Fetch response contracts.' This is a valid concern - the function accepts `() => any` and returns the response directly without type checking. However, this is more of a type safety/code quality issue rather than a bug that would cause runtime failures. The code will still work at runtime; it just loses TypeScript's compile-time type checking benefits. This is a legitimate code quality concern but falls into the category of a style/best practice issue rather than a concrete bug or security vulnerability that would cause the code to malfunction.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:13 — The type-erased parser throws on failure but returns a safe-parse envelope, producing inconsistent consumer behavior, credential corruption, and dead branches.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts, the function uses safeParse which returns {success: boolean, data?, error?}. When success is false, it throws an error. When success is true, it returns the safeParse result object (not just the data). The callers in GoogleCalendarService and Office365CalendarService use the return value differently - GoogleCalendarService passes it directly to prisma update as 'key', while Office365CalendarService destructures it expecting tokenResponse.success and tokenResponse.data. This is inconsistent - GoogleCalendarService would store the SafeParseReturnType object {success: true, data: {...}} instead of just the credential data, which would corrupt the stored credentials. This is a real bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:8 — The attempted generic schema uses unsupported computed keys and cannot preserve the fields required by the integrations it centralizes.
matched_golden_ids: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the same problem as the golden comment - it points to the same file (parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts) at line 8 and mentions 'unsupported computed keys' which is the same issue as the golden comment's description of 'computed property keys [z.string().toString()]' being invalid Zod syntax. Both are identifying that the schema uses invalid/unsupported computed key syntax.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:15 — Ambient global configuration selects validation independently of acquisition, silently coupling provider responses to the wrong schema.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts where APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED determines which schema is used for validation. Looking at the code, when credential sharing is enabled, it uses minimumTokenResponseSchema instead of the app-specific schema passed in. The concern is that this creates a coupling where the validation schema depends on a global config rather than the actual token source. However, this appears to be intentional design - when using credential sync, tokens come from a different endpoint (CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT) that returns a minimal response format, so using minimumTokenResponseSchema is correct for that case. The schema selection matches the token acquisition path. This is not a bug but rather the intended behavior for supporting two different token acquisition flows.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:13 — Raw sync responses are consumed as provider objects; Google stays expired and HubSpot may continue using stale module-global client state.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw response from either the credential sync endpoint or the refreshFunction. For Google Calendar (line 86-99), the code does `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` then `const token = res?.data` and `googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token`. However, when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true, refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response object (line 7-14), not the Google auth response with `.data` property. The code would try to access `response.data` on a fetch Response, which would be undefined, causing the token refresh to fail silently. This is a real bug - the return types are incompatible between the two code paths.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97 — Persisting the safe-parse wrapper removes top-level OAuth fields and breaks Google authentication after the first refresh.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for GoogleCalendarService.ts, line 97 shows `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);`. The parseRefreshTokenResponse function (in parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts) returns the result of safeParse, which is a ZodSafeParseReturnType object containing `success` and `data` properties, not the actual parsed data. The code then passes this wrapper object directly to `prisma.credential.update` as the `key` value. This would store `{success: true, data: {...}}` instead of the actual credential data, breaking authentication. This is a real bug - the code should be using `refreshTokenResponse.data` instead of the entire safeParse result.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:8 — The minimum schema silently discards expiration and provider metadata, causing refresh loops and incomplete persisted credentials.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts, the minimumTokenResponseSchema on lines 5-11 has a fundamental problem. The schema definition uses `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` as computed property keys, which doesn't work as intended in Zod - these would evaluate to literal string representations like '[object Object]' rather than creating dynamic property matchers. This means the schema only validates `access_token` exists but doesn't properly capture expiry fields. However, the finding claims it 'silently discards expiration and provider metadata' - but looking at line 24-26, if refresh_token is missing, it sets a placeholder value. The real issue is the schema syntax is incorrect and won't properly validate/capture expiry data, which could cause issues. But the finding's specific claim about 'refresh loops' is speculative - the code does attempt to handle the response and the schema issues would cause validation problems, not necessarily refresh loops. The schema syntax issue is real but the specific consequences described are somewhat speculative.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:9 — The sync request identifies credentials only by user and app despite multiple credentials being allowed, so it can refresh the wrong external account.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the refreshOAuthTokens function in packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts, it takes appSlug and userId as parameters and sends them to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT. The function is called from various calendar services (Google, Office365, Lark, Hubspot) passing credential.userId. However, the finding claims this could 'refresh the wrong external account' because a user might have multiple credentials for the same app. Examining the code: the sync endpoint receives calcomUserId and appSlug, and the comment says 'The response should only contain the access token and expiry date'. The actual credential update happens in the calling code (e.g., GoogleCalendarService) which uses the specific credential.id to update. The sync endpoint is just fetching new tokens - it's the external system's responsibility to know which account to refresh based on the user mapping. The finding assumes the external endpoint can't distinguish between multiple accounts, but this is a design choice for the external system, not a bug in this code. The code correctly passes the userId for the external system to handle.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — The token-returning sync endpoint is called without caller authentication, exposing fresh OAuth tokens to forged predictable-ID requests if reachable.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the refreshOAuthTokens function in packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts, when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is set, it makes a POST request to that endpoint with calcomUserId and appSlug in the body. The finding claims this lacks authentication, but examining the code, there's no authentication header being sent with this outbound request to the sync endpoint. However, this is an OUTBOUND request from Cal.com to an external endpoint that the self-hoster controls - it's not an inbound webhook. The security concern would be whether the external endpoint properly authenticates requests, but that's outside Cal.com's control. The actual security-sensitive inbound webhook (app-credential.ts) does have authentication via CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET header verification. The finding conflates the outbound token refresh request with the inbound credential sync webhook. The outbound request to fetch tokens doesn't need to authenticate itself to the external service in the same way - that's the external service's responsibility to secure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:73 — Credential updates have no event ID, version, timestamp, or compare-and-swap guard, allowing replayed or delayed webhooks to overwrite newer keys.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the webhook handler in apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts, the code does perform credential updates (lines 66-77) and creates (lines 78-86) without any idempotency checks, timestamps, or version guards. The webhook simply overwrites credentials based on userId and appId. However, this is a design choice for a credential sync feature, not necessarily a bug. The webhook is protected by a secret header check (lines 22-27), and the feature is designed for self-hosters syncing credentials from a parent application. While the finding raises a valid concern about replay attacks or out-of-order webhook delivery, this is more of a security hardening suggestion than a clear defect. The code functions as designed - it syncs credentials when called. Whether idempotency is required depends on the threat model and use case. This is a reasonable security concern but not a definitive bug in the implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:25 — The fabricated refresh-token sentinel overwrites Office 365’s valid token, preventing direct refresh if synchronization is disabled or unavailable.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts lines 23-25, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = 'refresh_token'` only when `!refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token` (i.e., when refresh_token is missing/falsy). This is a fallback for when the response doesn't include a refresh_token, not an overwrite of valid tokens. For Office 365, looking at office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts, the tokenResponse is spread into o365AuthCredentials which already contains the original refresh_token. If the new response has a refresh_token, it will be used; if not, the original is preserved. The finding claims it 'overwrites Office 365's valid token' but this is incorrect - it only sets a sentinel when no refresh_token exists in the response, and the original credentials are preserved through the spread operator. The concern about 'preventing direct refresh' is speculative and doesn't match the actual code flow.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:101 — The Salesforce connection is constructed with the stale pre-refresh access token, so the current operation can still fail after successful refresh.
matched_golden_ids: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment - that the Salesforce connection is being constructed with stale/pre-refresh access token values after a token refresh occurs. Both comments point to the same bug where the connection uses old credentials (credentialKey.access_token and credentialKey.instance_url) instead of the refreshed token values, which can lead to authentication failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62 — Non-atomic `findFirst` followed by `create` permits concurrent first deliveries to create duplicate credentials.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts lines 56-85, there's a findFirst query followed by either an update or create operation. If two concurrent webhook requests arrive for the same userId and appId combination, both could execute findFirst before either executes create, resulting in duplicate credentials being created. This is a real race condition - the code does `findFirst` at line 56, then based on whether `appCredential` exists, it either updates (line 66) or creates (line 76). Without a transaction or unique constraint enforcement, concurrent requests could both see null from findFirst and both proceed to create.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:31 — Throwing schema parsing is not translated into a defined 4xx response, so malformed client payloads receive internal-server errors.
matched_golden_ids: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

Both comments point to the same file, same line area, and same underlying issue of improper error handling for malformed payloads.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:17 — The mutating webhook does not constrain its HTTP method or return `405`/`Allow`, leaving callers without a stable method contract.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the webhook handler in apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts, the code does not check the HTTP method (req.method) before processing the request. The handler processes req.body which implies it expects POST requests, but it doesn't explicitly reject GET, PUT, DELETE, or other methods. This is a real issue - a webhook endpoint that modifies data (creates/updates credentials) should validate the HTTP method and return 405 Method Not Allowed for unsupported methods. This is a correctness and API contract issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62 — The non-atomic lookup/create flow and lack of uniqueness serialization allow duplicate credentials and arbitrary stale-row updates.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app-credential.ts lines 56-78, the flow is: 1) findFirst to check if credential exists, 2) if exists, update it, 3) if not, create it. This is indeed a non-atomic read-then-write pattern that could lead to race conditions. If two concurrent requests come in for the same userId/appId combination, both could pass the findFirst check (both finding no existing credential), and both would then attempt to create new credentials, potentially resulting in duplicate entries. However, looking at the Prisma schema context, there's no unique constraint shown on (userId, appId) combination for credentials, so duplicates could be created. This is a real concurrency/race condition issue that could cause duplicate credentials to be created.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:73 — Blind arrival-order updates allow delayed retries to overwrite newer credentials with older or revoked tokens.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the webhook endpoint in apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts, the code at lines 63-77 performs a findFirst to check if credentials exist, then either updates or creates them. The finding claims that 'blind arrival-order updates allow delayed retries to overwrite newer credentials with older or revoked tokens.' This is a valid concern - the endpoint has no mechanism to verify that incoming credentials are newer than existing ones (no timestamp comparison, no version checking, no idempotency key). If a webhook is retried or arrives out of order, older/stale credentials could overwrite newer valid ones. However, this is somewhat speculative about the operational context - it depends on how the external system sends webhooks. The code does perform a simple upsert pattern without any staleness protection, which is a real architectural concern for credential synchronization systems.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:31 — Validation, decryption, and JSON parsing failures are not mapped to 4xx responses, encouraging retries of poison requests and obscuring diagnosis.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts, line 31 uses `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` which throws a ZodError on validation failure. Lines 53-55 use `symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` which can throw errors. None of these are wrapped in try-catch blocks, so they will result in unhandled exceptions that typically return 500 Internal Server Error responses rather than appropriate 4xx client error responses. This is a real issue - validation failures should return 400 Bad Request, and decryption/parsing failures should return appropriate error codes to help clients understand what went wrong and avoid retrying poison requests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:75 — Salesforce refreshes unconditionally without a timeout and uses exact `statusText === "OK"` rather than `response.ok`, rejecting otherwise valid responses.
matched_golden_ids: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the same core problem as the golden comment - that the Salesforce integration uses `statusText === 'OK'` instead of `response.ok` for checking OAuth token refresh responses. Both comments point out that this approach can reject otherwise valid responses and lead to unreliable behavior. The candidate also mentions the same file location (CalendarService.ts) and the same underlying bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:31 — No request tests cover malformed bodies, invalid ciphertext, unsupported methods, or invalid decrypted JSON, leaving the endpoint’s error contract unprotected.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62 — No idempotency or concurrency test covers the separate lookup/create flow and resulting duplicate-credential risk.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a race condition in the credential creation flow at lines 62-92. adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62 — Concurrent first-time deliveries can create duplicates, after which later updates affect only an arbitrary credential row.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts lines 56-92, the logic is: findFirst to check if credential exists, then either update or create. This is a classic TOCTOU (time-of-check-time-of-use) race condition. If two concurrent webhook requests arrive for the same userId+appId combination when no credential exists yet, both will execute findFirst and get null, then both will attempt to create new credentials, resulting in duplicate rows. Subsequent updates would then use findFirst which returns an arbitrary row. This is a real concurrency bug in the new code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:25 — Mutating an omitted refresh token into the literal sentinel permanently breaks later provider fallback.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts lines 24-26, when refresh_token is missing from the response, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` (a literal string sentinel). This mutates the parsed response data. The function returns this modified response, and callers like Office365CalendarService use it to update credentials in the database. If the provider doesn't return a refresh_token (which is valid for some OAuth flows), the credential will be saved with the literal string "refresh_token" instead of preserving the original refresh_token. This would break subsequent token refreshes since the invalid sentinel would be used. This is a real bug - the code should preserve the original refresh_token from the credential rather than inserting a meaningless sentinel value.
